$comment: A GENERATED board of the REAL Earth: the ATLAS, the whole planet, the top of the three levels (Atlas > Region > Mini-map). `commission` is the only thing anybody writes by hand; `rows`, `settlements`, `regions`, `lessons` and the `plate` block are grown from it by `node tools/draw-map.mjs earth-atlas`, and the `atlas` block (winds, lanes, airship lines, ports) by `node tools/build-atlas.mjs`. Its land is not invented: `commission.earth` points at sampled real data (data/earth/atlas.samples.json, from tools/fetch-earth.mjs). Do not hand-edit the generated parts.
name: The Atlas
subtitle: the whole Earth, one time zone to a column, for ships and airships
summary: The real planet laid onto 24 columns of 15 degrees (the 24 time zones) and 14 rows of 11 degrees, about 1,400 km a hex. Ships sail it one hex a round and airships two, between real ports, on winds generated from the planet's real wind belts. A port inside a Region board opens onto that board; one outside is an abstract harbour.

commission.$comment: The input contract for a real-Earth board. Nothing here is invented: where the land is comes from sampled data, and what is typed is the window, the ports, the names and the lessons.
commission.why: The top of the three levels - Atlas, Region, Mini-map. Ships and airships travel on it for several rounds while the players' towns carry on, and it is the board the digital game navigates the whole world on. It teaches how the planet's winds go round its oceans, which is why the old trade routes went where they did.
commission.landmass: The whole Earth from 84 north to 73 south: every continent, the oceans between them, and the edge of the Antarctic ice. The board wraps: its east edge is its west edge, on the 180th meridian.
commission.$terrainBudgetNote: Left empty on purpose: a real place has no budget.
commission.$settlementNote: Real ports, placed at their real latitude and longitude. At 1,400 km a hex two ports a few hundred kilometres apart cannot both have a hex, which is why the list skips a few famous names.

routes.$note: The Atlas does not grow lanes the way a Region board does: its lanes are sailed on the winds, by tools/build-atlas.mjs.

earth.$comment: The Earth block. Everything here is a fact about the planet - a latitude, a longitude - and no hex is ever typed.
earth.$gridNote: Settled: 24 columns of 15 degrees (one time zone each, numbered across the top) by 14 rows of 11 degrees. The rows land on round numbers - row 7 is the equator, row 0 is 77 north, row 13 is 66 south - and the standard parallel, 32.1 degrees, is worked out from that by tools/lib/earth.mjs. One hex is about 1,412 km across at the standard parallel; at 77 degrees the same hex covers about a third of that east to west, and the sheet says so. On the even rows every column is centred on a time zone's own meridian - column 12 on Greenwich, column 0 on the 180th meridian, where the date changes - so the number across the top is the hours ahead of Greenwich. The odd rows sit half a hex east, as on every board, and straddle two zones.
earth.$zoomNote: Coarser than a Region board because a hex is a hundred times the area: zoom 4 is about 10 km a pixel for the sampler and zoom 5 about 5 km for the relief picture, which is finer than the plate can show.
earth.$riversNote: None on the board. At 1,400 km a hex a river would turn a hex the size of a country into a river; the relief picture still draws every big river, and a Region board puts them back.
earth.$forceNote: An island a player has heard of and a port needs, too small for a 1.7 million km2 hex to keep on its own. The tool reports what each one changed.
earth.$oceanSeedsNote: Points known to be open water: one in each ocean, and one in each sea a coarse sample might cut off at its strait (the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Baltic, the Red Sea, the Gulf). The Caspian is seeded as well: it is the world's biggest lake, salt, and below sea level.

lessons.title: Trade winds
lessons.text: Air that sinks at thirty degrees flows back towards the equator along the surface, and the Earth's spin turns it to blow from the east. Sailors could count on it every day of the year.

lessons.title: The doldrums
lessons.text: Where the trade winds of the two hemispheres meet, the air rises instead of blowing. A sailing ship could sit becalmed here for weeks.

lessons.title: Horse latitudes
lessons.text: Around thirty degrees the air sinks and the wind dies. The same sinking air makes the deserts on land at this latitude.

lessons.title: The westerlies
lessons.text: North of the high-pressure belt the wind blows from the west. Ships bound home to Europe ran north to find it.

lessons.title: Roaring Forties
lessons.text: In the far south no land stops the westerlies, so they blow harder than anywhere else. The clipper ships rode them from the Cape to Australia.

lessons.title: Monsoon
lessons.text: Land heats faster than sea. In summer the hot land of Asia draws wet sea air in; in winter the wind turns round and blows out.

lessons.title: Cape Horn
lessons.text: The bottom of the Americas, where the westerlies are squeezed between South America and Antarctica: the most feared corner of the sailing world.

lessons.title: Gulf Stream
lessons.text: A current of warm water from the Caribbean that runs up the American coast and across to Europe, which is why Britain is mild and Labrador, at the same latitude, is not.

lessons.title: How big an Atlas hex is
lessons.text: Each hex is fifteen degrees of longitude, one time zone, about 1,400 kilometres at the latitude the map is true at. Towards the poles the map stretches: up there a hex covers much less ground than it looks.

atlas.$comment: What makes this board the ATLAS: the top of the three levels (Atlas > Region > Mini-map). Read by tools/build-atlas.mjs, which grows the winds, the trade lanes and the airship lines from this and data/earth/winds.json, and writes them into the generated `atlas` block below. Ports are the commission `places`; whether a port is on a Region board or is an abstract harbour is worked out from the boards that exist, never typed.

moves.$note: Atlas hexes a round. One clock: the game is still 24 rounds, and a voyage takes several of them while the towns carry on.

plate.$note: Vector, so no long side to fall short of.

commission.$portsNote: The Mediterranean's own ports - Venice, Alexandria, Istanbul - are not on the Atlas: at 1,400 km a hex that sea is narrower than a hex and comes out as land. They are on the Mediterranean Region board, which opens off the Atlas at Lisbon. Jakarta shares Singapore's hex, and Halifax New York's, and both are left off for the same reason.

plate.$kindNote: Drawn by tools/draw-map.mjs from rows, not painted and traced. It is a build output: never hand-edited, regenerated by its tool, and safe to delete. A "drawn" plate is the opposite and the rules in docs/map/README.md are for that one.
plate.$fieldNote: Exact, because the tool chose it. On a drawn plate this is measured off the inner frame rule by eye and is the fiddliest step in the whole line.

relief.$note: A raster relief picture of the real ground, on the same pixels as this plate, with its layers beside it. The viewer and print page prefer it to the flat plate; tools/validate-map.mjs checks the files are there and the same size.

grid.$wrapNote: The east edge is the west edge. Every tool that walks this board steps from column 23 to column 0 and back; on a board without the flag nothing wraps.

print.$comment: Sheet layouts in the same three sizes as every other board. mapWidthMm, mapHeightMm and hexAcrossFlatsMm are derived and written in by tools/build-map.mjs.

presets.name: Four sheets, A2
presets.note: Two by two, printed landscape. The working size for a table.

presets.name: Nine sheets, A1
presets.note: Three by three. A vector plate prints at this size without asking.

presets.name: One sheet, reference
presets.note: The whole board on one page, for reading rather than playing.

legend.$comment: Character to terrain id, identical to the other two boards so a board from any map reads the same in a text editor.

$rowsNote: GENERATED by tools/draw-map.mjs from commission.landform. Do not hand-edit: run the tool. On a drawn map this block is traced off the artwork instead, and hand-correcting it is expected.
$riversNote: GENERATED. Each course is the chain of hexes the water runs through, spring first, and every one of those hexes is terrain `river` in rows. Run downhill by tools/draw-map.mjs from the terrain bands and the distance inland - never hand-placed, because a hand-placed river is how you get one that starts nowhere.

routes.$comment: Generated by tools/draw-map.mjs from the settlements and the water between them. A lane is the shortest walk a hull can make; a road only exists where two settlements share an island.

atlas.$comment: GENERATED by tools/build-atlas.mjs from commission.atlas, data/earth/winds.json and the land - do not hand-edit. What a game plays on the Atlas: every port and what it opens onto, the wind in every hex, every trade lane and airship line as a chain of hexes with its cost in rounds. The rules that turn these into moves are docs/js/atlas.js; the wind rule they use is the EXAMPLE in data/earth/winds.json, not an adopted rule.

moves.$note: Atlas hexes a round. One clock: the game is still 24 rounds, and a voyage takes several of them while the towns carry on.

winds.$comment: One per hex: [col, row, bearing the wind blows TOWARD (compass degrees, north up the board), speed m/s, belt]. Averaged over the hex's sea; a hex with no sea takes the belt's own wind. Calm below data/earth/winds.json calmBelowMs.

exampleRule.$comment: AN EXAMPLE, NOT A RULE YET. What a step of one Atlas hex costs a sailing ship, in rounds, by the wind in the hex it leaves. It is here so the lanes can be sailed and the digital game can try it; no rules chapter prints it until it is adopted.
exampleRule.how: Take the angle between the way the ship steps and the way the wind blows. Straight downwind costs withWind, square across costs across, dead into it costs againstWind, smoothly between; a wind weaker than fullStrengthMs moves the cost only that share of the way from across. A calm hex costs calm whichever way the ship goes.

lanes.note: Out of Europe with the trade winds, a long swing towards Brazil, then round the Cape for India.

lanes.name: Manila Galleon
lanes.note: West across the Pacific on the trade winds.

lanes.name: Galleon homeward
lanes.note: Home again: north to the westerlies first.

lanes.name: The Treasure Fleet
lanes.note: Gathered at Havana and rode the westerlies home.

lanes.name: The Clipper Route
lanes.note: South through the trades, then the Roaring Forties east.

lanes.name: Round the Horn
lanes.note: The gold-rush run round South America.

lanes.name: Spice Route
lanes.note: The old sea road from Arabia to China.

airships.name: The Polar Line
airships.note: The shortest way from London to California is over Greenland - a straight line on a globe looks like an arch on a flat map.
